claims.text: Test-set performance scores alone are insufficient for drawing accurate conclusions about which machine learning model performs best.
Under uniform random hyperparameter search, the expected maximum validation performance given a budget of n trials can be calculated in closed form using empirical cumulative distribution functions.
Calculating expected maximum validation performance in closed form has strictly less error than bootstrap estimation because it eliminates resampling error.
For hyperparameter search budgets under 10 assignments on 5-way Stanford Sentiment Treebank classification, logistic regression achieves higher expected validation accuracy than a CNN.
For hyperparameter search budgets exceeding 10 assignments on 5-way Stanford Sentiment Treebank classification, a CNN achieves higher expected validation accuracy than logistic regression.
Matching the reported development exact match score for BiDAF on SQuAD using random hyperparameter search requires an estimated budget of 18 GPU days (55 hyperparameter trials).
None of 50 randomly selected EMNLP 2018 papers with experimental results reported all items in the proposed experimental reporting checklist.

evidence.description: Model comparisons across SST, SciTail, and SQuAD demonstrate that changing the hyperparameter evaluation budget alters which model family achieves superior performance.
Equation 8 presents the plug-in estimator for E[V*_n|n] based on empirical cumulative probabilities P(Vi <= v) and P(Vi < v) derived from n i.i.d. random hyperparameter draws.
Bootstrap estimation incurs both finite sample error and resampling error from K repeated resamples, whereas the proposed closed-form calculation retains only finite sample error.
Figure 1 shows expected validation accuracy curves where logistic regression outperforms CNN when evaluating x <= 10 hyperparameter assignments.
Figure 1 shows the CNN expected validation accuracy curve surpassing logistic regression when evaluating x > 10 hyperparameter assignments.
Figure 4 shows that the expected validation exact match curve for BiDAF reaches the original paper's reported score at 55 hyperparameter trials, equivalent to 18 GPU days of training duration.

An empirical audit of 50 randomly sampled EMNLP 2018 papers found 0% coverage for the full 10-item experimental checklist, with 10% or fewer papers reporting hyperparameter search bounds or number of search trials.

methodologies.name: Expected Validation Performance Curves
methodologies.description: A diagnostic method computing the expected maximum validation performance as a function of computational budget n using empirical cumulative distribution functions from random hyperparameter trials.
conditions: Uniform random sampling of hyperparameter values
Closed-form estimation without additional model training beyond hyperparameter search

limitations.text: Current reporting practices in machine learning rely on single point-estimates of test performance without reporting computational budgets or hyperparameter search details.
Using the bootstrap to estimate mean and variance of best validation performance introduces resampling error.

The proposed analytical estimation requires hyperparameter trials to be drawn i.i.d. (e.g., via random search), making it inapplicable to adaptive search strategies like Bayesian optimization or manual tuning.
The method does not extrapolate performance to computational budgets larger than the actual number of evaluated trials N.

future_work.text: Forecasting model validation performance for larger computational budgets n > N beyond the observed hyperparameter evaluations.
